captain-inspection-sailors-rows-deck.head: On Saturday, the sixth of December 1941, the battleships held their usual weekly inspections.
captain-inspection-sailors-rows-deck.body: The sixth of December was a fine, clear day on Oahu, with light trade winds. At Pearl Harbor, Saturday morning brought the regular weekly inspection aboard the battleships. Crews stood in rows on deck in their best white uniforms. Commanding officers walked along the lines, checking uniforms, shoes and haircuts. They then inspected living spaces, sometimes running a white-gloved finger along shelves to look for dust. Navy regulations required such inspections to maintain discipline and cleanliness. After inspection, many men were granted liberty for the rest of the weekend. Ship logs and personal accounts describe the day as calm and routine. Many sailors spent the afternoon ashore. Even so, a portion of every crew remained aboard on duty. Historians often use this Saturday to illustrate how normal life appeared at Pearl Harbor less than a day before the attack. Nothing in the routine suggested that anything unusual was about to happen.

department-store-christmas-tinsel-palms.head: In Honolulu, department stores were decorated for Christmas, and Santa Claus received children in the warm sunshine.
department-store-christmas-tinsel-palms.body: By early December, Honolulu's shopping streets were busy with Christmas shoppers. Department stores displayed tinsel, paper bells and other decorations, and played carols about snow and sleigh bells. A Santa Claus in a heavy red suit received children in the stores, despite the warm weather. Families bought toys and books and wrapped presents for the holiday. Many had ordered gifts from the mainland months in advance, hoping they would arrive by ship in time. Newspaper advertisements from the first week of December 1941 show sales, gift suggestions and holiday events. Historians use these advertisements to illustrate everyday life on the eve of the war. The contrast between the cold-weather imagery of Christmas and the tropical setting was often noted by visitors. Even so, island families had developed their own customs, mixing mainland traditions with local food and flowers. For most residents, the holiday season of 1941 began in an entirely ordinary way.

football-stadium-crowd-sunny-afternoon.head: On the afternoon of the sixth of December, about twenty-four thousand people watched a football game in Honolulu.
football-stadium-crowd-sunny-afternoon.body: On Saturday afternoon, the University of Hawaii played Willamette University, from Salem, Oregon, in a game called the Shrine Bowl. It took place at Honolulu Stadium, and about twenty-four thousand spectators attended. The Willamette team had travelled to Hawaii by ship for the occasion. The University of Hawaii won the game. Newspapers the next morning reported on it. The visiting players planned to stay in Hawaii for several more days, and some were due to play another game the following week. After the attack, those plans were cancelled. Several Willamette players and fans helped with defence work and volunteered in the days that followed, before returning home weeks later. Historians and the universities themselves have recorded the story in later years. The game shows how many civilians from the mainland were present in Honolulu that weekend. To the crowd in the stadium, it was simply a sunny afternoon of college football.

waikiki-saturday-families-picnic-sand.head: On the last Saturday before the attack, many families spent the afternoon at Waikiki Beach.
waikiki-saturday-families-picnic-sand.body: Waikiki Beach was crowded on the afternoon of the sixth of December. Families had picnics on the sand, and children swam in the calm water inside the reef. Beachboys taught visitors to surf and took them out in outrigger canoes. Off-duty servicemen joined the crowds. As the afternoon went on, the shadows of the palm trees grew longer across the beach. Families packed up and went home as the sun set behind the mountains. Photographs taken that weekend, some now held in museums, show ordinary scenes of leisure on the beach. Many people who were children at the time later recalled it in interviews. They often described it as their last memory of peacetime Hawaii. Historians emphasise that such memories help explain how sudden the change was. Within a day, beaches would be closed and lined with barbed wire. Yet on that Saturday, Waikiki looked as it had for years, relaxed and sunlit.

band-on-stage-arena-sailors-dancing.head: On the evening of the sixth of December, a round of the Battle of Music was held at Bloch Arena.
band-on-stage-arena-sailors-dancing.body: On Saturday evening, sailors crowded into Bloch Arena at the Navy Yard for another round of the Battle of Music. Several ships' bands competed, and the audience danced and cheered. The band of the Pennsylvania won that evening's competition, according to accounts from the period. The Arizona's band had already qualified in an earlier round. When the contest ended, those present reportedly sang God Bless America together, a popular song at the time. Many of the musicians returned to their ships for the night. The final competition was scheduled for the twentieth of December. It never took place. Survivors later spoke about the evening in oral history interviews. They remembered the music, the dancing and the friendly rivalry between ships. Even so, for many of those present, it was the last evening of their lives. Historians often mention the event because it captures the atmosphere at Pearl Harbor only hours before the attack.

moonlit-harbour-battleships-silhouettes.head: On the night of the sixth of December, the harbour was calm under a bright moon.
moonlit-harbour-battleships-silhouettes.body: The night of the sixth of December was clear over Oahu. The moon, a few days past full, lit the harbour. The battleships lay in their usual places along Battleship Row, their outlines visible against the water. Most of the crews had returned from liberty by midnight. Watchstanders remained on duty while the rest of the men slept. The Navy Yard was quiet, apart from the normal sounds of a large base at night. Hundreds of miles to the north, the Japanese carrier force was steaming south toward its launch position. Historians reconstructing the events note that the attack force was then about two hundred and thirty miles from Oahu by early morning. In Honolulu, most residents were asleep. Some nightclubs and dance halls stayed open late. Survivors who remembered that night often described it as peaceful and beautiful. The harbour showed no sign of what was about to happen.

sunday-dawn-oahu-mountains-clouds-pink.head: Sunday, the seventh of December 1941, dawned calm and clear over Oahu.
sunday-dawn-oahu-mountains-clouds-pink.body: Sunrise on the seventh of December came a little before seven o'clock. The weather was mild, with scattered clouds over the mountains and light winds. Most military personnel were not on duty, since it was Sunday. Many slept late after Saturday night. On the ships, the duty sections were preparing for the morning routine. In Honolulu and the surrounding towns, families prepared breakfast and got ready for church. Radio stations played music. Weather records and many personal accounts describe an unusually pleasant morning. Survivors later remembered details such as the softness of the light and the smell of breakfast. Historians reconstructing the morning use logs, reports and testimony to establish the times of events. By then, the first wave of Japanese aircraft had already taken off from the carriers to the north, at about six o'clock. Even so, nobody on Oahu knew it. For a short time longer, the morning remained entirely ordinary.

small-destroyer-patrol-calm-sea-dawn.head: Early on the seventh of December, the destroyer Ward fired on a small submarine near the harbour entrance.
small-destroyer-patrol-calm-sea-dawn.body: The USS Ward was an old destroyer patrolling the entrance to Pearl Harbor. At about a quarter to seven on the morning of the seventh of December, its crew spotted a small submarine trying to follow another ship into the harbour. The Ward opened fire and dropped depth charges. The submarine sank. It was one of five Japanese midget submarines sent to take part in the attack. These were the first American shots of the Pacific War. The Ward's commander reported the action to headquarters. However, the message took time to reach senior officers, and earlier false alarms had made some officials cautious. No general alert followed. In 2002, researchers from the University of Hawaii found the wreck of the midget submarine on the seabed outside the harbour, with a shell hole in its tower. The discovery confirmed the Ward's account. Historians still discuss how this early warning might have changed events if it had been acted on.

radar-station-hilltop-north-shore-dawn.head: At the Opana radar station, two young soldiers stayed on duty after their shift to practise with the equipment.
radar-station-hilltop-north-shore-dawn.body: The army operated several new mobile radar stations on Oahu in 1941. One was at Opana, on a hill near the northern tip of the island. On the morning of the seventh of December, it was staffed by two privates, Joseph Lockard and George Elliott. Their scheduled watch ended at seven o'clock. Because the truck to take them to breakfast was late, they kept the radar running to give Elliott more practice. At about two minutes past seven, they saw an unusually large signal on the screen. It indicated many aircraft about a hundred and thirty miles to the north. Radar was still very new, and operators were inexperienced. Lockard and Elliott checked their equipment and then telephoned the information centre at Fort Shafter. Historians regard their observation as one of the most important missed warnings of the day. The original Opana radar set is now preserved in a museum.

young-soldiers-radar-screen-hut.head: The officer who received the radar report believed the aircraft were American bombers expected from California.
young-soldiers-radar-screen-hut.body: The call from Opana reached the information centre at Fort Shafter, where a young officer, Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, was on duty. He was a fighter pilot with little training in the new radar system. A flight of American B-17 bombers was expected that morning from California. Tyler assumed the signal was those aircraft and told the radar operators not to worry about it. The radar operators continued tracking the signal until it was lost near the island. Later investigations concluded that Tyler had acted on the information available to him. The information centre was not yet fully operational, and procedures were still being developed. Historians note that even a warning of thirty or forty minutes might have allowed some preparation. Even so, many defences would still have needed time to be readied. The B-17s did arrive that morning, unarmed and low on fuel, in the middle of the attack. Several were damaged while landing.

plantation-village-church-bell-sunday.head: Across Oahu, Sunday morning began with church bells and families preparing for the day.
plantation-village-church-bell-sunday.body: In towns and plantation villages across Oahu, the seventh of December started like any Sunday. Church bells rang for morning services. Families ironed clothes, prepared breakfast and listened to the radio. Children played outside. In Honolulu, newspapers were delivered and shops were mostly closed. Many military families on the bases were still asleep or having a late breakfast. Oral history projects in Hawaii have collected hundreds of memories of that morning. People often recall precise details, such as what they were eating or doing when they first heard unusual noises. Historians value these accounts because they show how the attack affected civilians as well as servicemen. Most residents of Oahu were not directly in danger, but many saw or heard the attack. Some civilians were killed, mostly by anti-aircraft shells that fell on Honolulu. Before eight o'clock, however, the island was quiet. Daily life seemed settled, and the holidays were approaching.

sailors-on-deck-soft-morning-light-ships.head: On the morning of the seventh of December, Dorie Miller was collecting laundry aboard the West Virginia.
sailors-on-deck-soft-morning-light-ships.body: Aboard the battleship West Virginia, mess attendant Doris Miller rose at about six o'clock, as usual. According to later accounts, he was collecting laundry from officers' quarters when the attack began. Across the harbour, other sailors were at breakfast, preparing for church services or resting on deck. Duty sections were carrying out the normal Sunday routine. The West Virginia was moored outboard of the Tennessee on Battleship Row. Navy records and survivor testimony allow historians to place many individual sailors at particular locations that morning. Miller's own later statements and the citation for his medal describe his actions after the attack began. Even so, details of his exact movements vary between accounts. Before eight o'clock, his morning was like that of hundreds of other mess attendants. The routine tasks of a large ship were underway. Within minutes, the situation aboard every battleship would change completely.

flag-detail-stern-morning-band-ready.head: At about a quarter to eight, colour guards on the ships prepared to raise the flags at eight o'clock.
flag-detail-stern-morning-band-ready.body: Raising the colours, the national flag, was a daily naval ceremony performed at eight o'clock in the morning. On the seventh of December, colour guards and bands assembled on the sterns of many ships shortly before eight. The bands were ready to play the national anthem as the flags rose. On the Nevada, the band and colour guard were in place at the stern. Similar preparations were taking place across the harbour. Navy regulations prescribed the ceremony in detail, and it was carried out every day, in port or at sea. Survivor accounts often mention that they were waiting for the eight o'clock ceremony when the first aircraft appeared. The first bombs fell at about five minutes to eight. Historians use the ceremony as a fixed reference point for the timeline of the attack. It also shows how closely ordinary routine and sudden war met that morning, within a few minutes of each other.

distant-planes-over-green-hills-morning.head: When the first aircraft appeared, many people on Oahu thought they were watching a Sunday training exercise.
distant-planes-over-green-hills-morning.body: The first wave of Japanese aircraft reached Oahu shortly before eight o'clock. Military exercises with aircraft were common, so many people who saw planes overhead at first assumed they were American. Survivors frequently said they did not realise what was happening until they saw explosions or the red circle markings on the aircraft. At about five minutes to eight, the attack began on airfields and on the ships in the harbour. Aircraft at Hickam Field, Wheeler Field and other bases were attacked so that they could not take off. Within minutes, the harbour was under attack. A message sent from Ford Island, announcing an air raid and stating that it was not a drill, was broadcast soon afterwards. Historians have reconstructed the timeline from logs, photographs and testimony. Even so, accounts of the first moments differ. Confusion was common. Many people struggled to believe that an attack was really taking place on such a peaceful morning.

navy-band-stern-flag-morning-sun.head: On the Nevada, the band continued playing the national anthem as the attack began.
navy-band-stern-flag-morning-sun.body: Aboard the battleship Nevada, the band was on the stern to play the national anthem for the eight o'clock flag ceremony. As the band began to play, Japanese aircraft flew over the ship. According to accounts from crew members, the band continued playing until the anthem was finished before taking cover. The flag was raised as planned. Survivor testimony and later histories of the ship record this event. It has been retold many times as an example of discipline and composure. Historians note that some details, such as exact timing, vary between accounts. Even so, the core of the story is widely accepted. The moment reflected the strength of naval routine and training. Members of the band then took up emergency duties, as bandsmen were trained to do in an emergency. Several were assigned to help with ammunition and damage control during the rest of the attack. The episode remains one of the best-known moments of that morning.

battleship-leaving-channel-flag-flying.head: The Nevada was the only battleship to get underway during the attack.
battleship-leaving-channel-flag-flying.body: The Nevada was moored at the northern end of Battleship Row. Its crew managed to raise steam and get the ship moving during the attack, a process that normally took much longer. With many senior officers ashore, junior officers and enlisted men took charge. The battleship moved down the channel toward the harbour entrance. It came under heavy attack during the second wave. To avoid sinking in the narrow channel and blocking the harbour, the Nevada was deliberately run aground near Hospital Point. Later, it was moved to the other side of the channel. Navy records and survivor accounts describe the effort in detail. Historians regard the Nevada's movement as one of the most notable actions of the day. The ship was repaired and returned to service. In 1944, it supported the landings in Normandy. The Nevada's crew received several awards for their actions on the seventh of December.

quiet-sky-over-harbour-late-morning-haze.head: The attack lasted less than two hours and was over by about ten o'clock in the morning.
quiet-sky-over-harbour-late-morning-haze.body: The Japanese attack came in two waves. The first began shortly before eight o'clock, and the second arrived about an hour later. By about ten o'clock, the last aircraft had left, returning to the carriers to the north. The Japanese commanders decided not to launch a third attack. In less than two hours, eight American battleships had been damaged, and several were sunk or capsized. Many other ships and more than three hundred aircraft were destroyed or damaged. A total of two thousand four hundred and three Americans were killed, including sixty-eight civilians. More than one thousand one hundred of the dead were aboard the Arizona. Historians note that important targets, such as fuel storage tanks and repair facilities, were largely untouched. The American aircraft carriers were also at sea. These factors affected the course of the war that followed. On Oahu, the morning ended in smoke and silence, as people began rescue and recovery work.

big-young-sailor-carrying-shipmate-deck.head: Dorie Miller, who had no training on anti-aircraft guns, helped carry wounded men and then fired a machine gun.
big-young-sailor-carrying-shipmate-deck.body: When the West Virginia was hit by torpedoes and bombs, Miller went to help. According to his medal citation and later accounts, he helped carry wounded sailors to safety, including the ship's captain, Mervyn Bennion, who was mortally wounded. Miller was then ordered to help with a machine gun. As a mess attendant, he had never been trained to operate one. He fired the gun at attacking aircraft until he was ordered to leave the ship. The West Virginia sank in shallow water. Miller's actions were first reported without his name. The Black press, especially the Pittsburgh Courier, campaigned to identify him and to see him recognised. In 1942, he was awarded the Navy Cross. Historians note that his story became important to the civil rights movement. It showed both courage and the injustice of the restrictions placed on Black sailors. Even so, Miller himself spoke modestly about what he had done that morning.

sailor-hangar-ramp-kaneohe-bay-morning.head: At Kaneohe Bay, Chief Petty Officer John Finn fired a machine gun for more than two hours despite many wounds.
sailor-hangar-ramp-kaneohe-bay-morning.body: The naval air station at Kaneohe Bay, on the windward side of Oahu, was attacked shortly before the main assault on Pearl Harbor. John Finn, a chief aviation ordnanceman, was at home with his wife when the attack began. He drove to the station and set up a machine gun on an exposed position near the seaplane ramps. He fired at attacking aircraft for more than two hours. During this time, he was wounded more than twenty times. After receiving medical treatment, he returned to help rearm aircraft. In 1942, Finn was awarded the Medal of Honor. He was the first American in the Second World War to receive it for actions on the seventh of December. Finn lived to the age of a hundred, dying in 2010. He was the last living Medal of Honor recipient from the attack. In interviews, he insisted that he had simply done his job, as many others had done that day.

navy-nurses-hospital-ward-white-uniforms.head: Navy nurse Ruth Erickson later recalled that the wounded men were quiet and brave, and asked first about their friends.
navy-nurses-hospital-ward-white-uniforms.body: On the morning of the seventh of December, Ruth Erickson was a young navy nurse at the Naval Hospital at Pearl Harbor. She was having breakfast when the attack began. Within minutes, wounded men began arriving at the hospital. Nurses, doctors and corpsmen worked without rest throughout the day and night. Many patients had severe burns. Erickson later gave a detailed oral history interview to the Navy. She described the calm and courage of the injured sailors, many of whom asked about their shipmates before themselves. The hospital was quickly overwhelmed, and additional space was used for treatment. Navy nurses from other facilities and civilian volunteers helped. Historians use accounts like Erickson's to describe the medical response to the attack. Even so, the nurses rarely spoke about their own exhaustion. Their work continued for many weeks. Erickson's testimony is now part of the Navy's historical archive and is often quoted in histories of the day.

volunteers-line-blood-bank-honolulu.head: After the attack, so many people volunteered to give blood that collection supplies ran short.
volunteers-line-blood-bank-honolulu.body: In the hours after the attack, hospitals across Oahu needed large amounts of blood. Earlier in 1941, doctors in Honolulu had organised a blood bank, which proved vital. Radio announcements asked for donors, and long lines formed outside hospitals and donation centres. People of every background came forward, including many Japanese American residents. According to accounts from the period, there were more volunteers than containers to collect their blood. Additional bottles had to be found and sterilised. Historians of the medical response note how quickly civilians organised to help. Doctors from Honolulu also went to military hospitals to assist. Local newspapers later praised the response. Even so, conditions remained difficult for days, as hospitals cared for many seriously injured patients. The blood donation effort showed the community's support for the wounded. It also demonstrated that people of Japanese ancestry in Hawaii were part of the island's response, a point that became important in the months that followed.

workers-small-boat-ship-hull-tools.head: Rescuers cut through the hull of the capsized Oklahoma and freed thirty-two trapped sailors.
workers-small-boat-ship-hull-tools.body: The battleship Oklahoma was struck by several torpedoes and capsized within minutes. Many crew members were trapped inside the overturned hull. Rescuers on the surface heard tapping from inside. Civilian workers from the Navy Yard, along with sailors, began cutting through the steel bottom of the ship. The work was dangerous and slow. Cutting torches could ignite fuel or consume the air in the compartments. Workers used drills and chisels where possible. Over the following day and night, they rescued thirty-two men. Julio DeCastro, a civilian yard worker, led one of the main rescue teams. His team was later recognised for its efforts. Survivors described seeing daylight through the hole in the hull as one of the most powerful moments of their lives. Historians note that four hundred and twenty-nine men from the Oklahoma died. Even so, the rescues saved lives that would otherwise have been lost.

harbour-small-boats-afternoon-calm-light.head: During and after the attack, many small boats, including private craft, helped rescue men from the water.
harbour-small-boats-afternoon-calm-light.body: When ships were hit and burning oil spread across the harbour, many sailors were thrown or jumped into the water. Small boats from ships and shore stations went to pick them up. Launches, motor whaleboats and tugboats carried survivors to safety and took the wounded to hospitals. Some privately owned boats and fishing craft also joined the rescue efforts. Survivors later described being pulled from the water by people they never saw again. Navy reports from the following days record many acts of rescue by boat crews. Historians point out that much of this work was done by people with no formal orders, acting on their own initiative. Even so, the burning oil made rescue very dangerous. Many rescuers were later decorated. Others were never formally recognised. Their efforts saved many lives during the attack and in the hours that followed, as smoke continued to cover parts of the harbour.

blackout-house-candle-family-night.head: On the night of the seventh of December, a blackout was imposed across Oahu.
blackout-house-candle-family-night.body: On the afternoon of the seventh of December, the governor of Hawaii declared martial law, and the army took control of the territory. That night, a complete blackout was ordered across Oahu. All lights had to be turned off or covered. Cars drove without headlights, and windows were blacked out. Many people feared another attack or an invasion. Rumours spread quickly, and nervous sentries fired at shadows. Some American aircraft returning that night were fired on by mistake. With the town and bases dark, the night sky was unusually clear. Many residents later remembered the brightness of the stars. Oral history accounts describe families sitting together in darkened rooms, listening to the radio for news. Historians note that martial law remained in place in Hawaii until October 1944. Blackouts and curfews became part of daily life for many months. The first night set the pattern for this long period of restrictions.

workers-factory-gathered-around-radio.head: On the eighth of December, President Roosevelt addressed Congress, and millions listened on the radio.
workers-factory-gathered-around-radio.body: On Monday, the eighth of December, President Franklin Roosevelt spoke to a joint session of Congress. He described the seventh of December as a date which will live in infamy. His speech lasted only a few minutes. It was broadcast nationwide, and historians estimate that it reached the largest radio audience in American history up to that time. Factories, offices and schools paused so that people could listen. Within an hour, Congress declared war on Japan, with only one dissenting vote. Three days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. The country was now fully involved in the Second World War. Historians often describe the attack as a turning point in American public opinion. Before it, many Americans opposed entering the war. Afterwards, enlistment offices were crowded with volunteers. Even so, many families also prepared for long separations. The speech remains one of the most famous in American history.

honolulu-christmas-1941-quiet-blackout.head: Christmas 1941 in Hawaii was celebrated quietly, under blackout and martial law.
honolulu-christmas-1941-quiet-blackout.body: Christmas came less than three weeks after the attack. In Hawaii, the blackout continued, and Christmas lights could not be used outdoors. Families decorated their trees indoors, behind blackout curtains. Many military families had lost relatives or were preparing to leave for the mainland. Parcels and letters from the mainland were delayed by wartime shipping restrictions. Churches held services, though evening gatherings were limited by the curfew. Newspapers carried messages encouraging residents to keep up their spirits. Oral history interviews describe a subdued holiday, with small gatherings and simple meals. Historians note that many residents also helped wounded servicemen and families affected by the attack. Volunteers organised gifts for patients in hospitals. Even so, the mood was serious. Nobody knew how long the war would last. For many families in Hawaii, Christmas 1941 was remembered as a time of uncertainty, but also of quiet kindness within the community.

young-soldiers-hawaii-families-farewell-.head: Thousands of Japanese Americans from Hawaii later served in the army, many in units with the motto Go for Broke.
young-soldiers-hawaii-families-farewell-.body: After the attack, Japanese Americans faced suspicion and discrimination. On the mainland, more than one hundred and ten thousand people of Japanese ancestry were forcibly removed and held in camps. In Hawaii, where they made up more than a third of the population, mass removal was not carried out, though some community leaders were detained. Many young Japanese Americans in Hawaii sought to prove their loyalty. Soldiers of Japanese ancestry already in the Hawaii National Guard formed the 100th Infantry Battalion. In 1943, the army formed the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, and thousands of volunteers from Hawaii joined. Its motto was Go for Broke, a phrase from island gambling slang meaning to risk everything. The 100th and the 442nd fought in Italy and France. Historians describe them as among the most highly decorated American units of their size in the war. Their record later helped change attitudes toward Japanese Americans across the country.

white-house-lawn-christmas-tree-evening.head: On Christmas Eve 1941, Winston Churchill joined President Roosevelt at the lighting of the national Christmas tree.
white-house-lawn-christmas-tree-evening.body: British Prime Minister Winston Churchill travelled to Washington in December 1941 to meet President Roosevelt and plan the joint war effort. He stayed at the White House over Christmas. On Christmas Eve, the two leaders appeared together at the lighting of the national Christmas tree on the White House grounds. A large crowd attended. Both men spoke to the crowd and to radio listeners. Churchill addressed the children of America, encouraging them to enjoy their Christmas despite the war. Recordings and transcripts of the speeches survive. Historians often cite the occasion as a symbol of the new alliance between Britain and the United States. After that evening, the tree remained unlit for the rest of the war, because of wartime blackout rules. The joint meeting, known as the Arcadia Conference, produced important decisions about strategy. Churchill also addressed the United States Congress on the twenty-sixth of December.

admiral-nimitz-arriving-flying-boat-harb.head: Admiral Chester Nimitz arrived at Pearl Harbor on Christmas morning 1941 to take command of the Pacific Fleet.
admiral-nimitz-arriving-flying-boat-harb.body: After the attack, Admiral Kimmel was relieved of command. President Roosevelt chose Admiral Chester Nimitz, from Texas, to replace him. Nimitz travelled across the country and then flew to Hawaii in a navy flying boat. He arrived at Pearl Harbor on the morning of the twenty-fifth of December, 1941, in the rain. Officers who met him later said he spoke little and took in the damage carefully. He formally took command on the thirty-first of December, in a ceremony aboard a submarine. Nimitz decided to keep most of Kimmel's staff, which helped morale. Historians credit him with steady and effective leadership throughout the war. Under his command, the Pacific Fleet won major victories, including the Battle of Midway in June 1942. On the second of September 1945, Nimitz signed the Japanese surrender document aboard the battleship Missouri. The Missouri is now moored at Pearl Harbor, near the Arizona Memorial.

salvage-divers-harbour-calm-morning.head: Navy divers worked for months in dark, oily water to raise and repair the sunken ships.
salvage-divers-harbour-calm-morning.body: After the attack, the navy began a large salvage operation at Pearl Harbor. Divers worked in heavy canvas suits and brass helmets, supplied with air from the surface. The water in the harbour was dark and covered with oil, so divers often worked by touch. They sealed holes, removed ammunition and recovered bodies. Engineers pumped water out of the damaged ships so that they could be refloated and repaired. The work continued for more than a year. Navy records describe thousands of hours of diving. Several divers lost their lives in accidents during the operation. Historians describe the salvage effort as one of the largest of its kind ever undertaken. Captain Homer Wallin, who led much of the work, later wrote a detailed account of it. The Oklahoma was righted in 1943 but was never returned to service. The Arizona was judged beyond repair and left in place, where it remains today.

grey-battleships-at-sea-sunset-pacific.head: Six of the eight battleships damaged at Pearl Harbor were repaired and returned to service.
grey-battleships-at-sea-sunset-pacific.body: Of the eight battleships damaged in the attack, only the Arizona and the Oklahoma were permanently lost. The other six, the California, the Maryland, the Nevada, the Pennsylvania, the Tennessee and the West Virginia, were repaired. Some needed only minor work and returned to service within weeks. Others, such as the California and the West Virginia, had sunk in shallow water and required major reconstruction. They returned to the fleet in 1944, extensively modernised. Several of these ships took part in later battles. In October 1944, at the Battle of Surigao Strait in the Philippines, five Pearl Harbor survivors were part of the battle line that defeated a Japanese force. Historians often mention this as a striking turn in the story. The ships that had been sunk or damaged at their moorings later fought at sea. The skill of the repair workers at Pearl Harbor and on the mainland made this possible.

medal-ceremony-carrier-deck-1942-sun.head: Dorie Miller became the first Black American to receive the Navy Cross.
medal-ceremony-carrier-deck-1942-sun.body: On the twenty-seventh of May, 1942, Admiral Chester Nimitz presented Doris Miller with the Navy Cross aboard the aircraft carrier Enterprise at Pearl Harbor. It was then the navy's third-highest award for bravery. Miller was the first Black American to receive it. Nimitz said that the award was the first of its kind to a member of his race in this conflict and would not be the last. Miller later took part in a war bond tour in the United States. He was then assigned to the escort carrier Liscome Bay. On the twenty-fourth of November, 1943, the ship was sunk by a Japanese submarine near the Gilbert Islands, and Miller was among those lost. In 2020, the navy announced that a future aircraft carrier would be named the USS Doris Miller. Historians note that it will be the first aircraft carrier named after a Black American and the first named after an enlisted sailor for actions in the Second World War.

elderly-woman-telling-story-living-room.head: Ruth Erickson, who nursed the wounded at Pearl Harbor, later became director of the Navy Nurse Corps.
elderly-woman-telling-story-living-room.body: After the attack, Ruth Erickson continued her career in the Navy Nurse Corps. She served at hospitals in the United States and overseas during and after the war, including during the Korean War. Over the years, she rose through the ranks. From 1962 to 1966, she served as director of the Navy Nurse Corps, the highest position in the corps. In later life, she gave oral history interviews describing her experiences on the seventh of December and in her long career. These recordings are now held by the Navy's history programmes and are widely used by historians and museums. She described the nurses' work with care and modesty. Historians note that the role of women in the medical response to the attack was for many years less widely known. Accounts like hers have helped change that. Erickson died in 2008. Her life spanned the period from the attack to the modern navy, in which women serve in nearly every role.

japanese-farmer-rice-field-evening-1950s.head: Mitsuo Fuchida, who led the Japanese air attack, later became a Christian evangelist and visited the United States many times.
japanese-farmer-rice-field-evening-1950s.body: Commander Mitsuo Fuchida led the first wave of the attack on Pearl Harbor. He survived the war, during which he took part in several major battles. After the surrender, he returned to his home village and worked as a farmer for a time. In 1950, he converted to Christianity, influenced in part by the story of an American former prisoner of war who had become a missionary. Fuchida then travelled widely as an evangelist. He visited the United States many times, speaking about reconciliation and forgiveness. He also met some American veterans of the war. He wrote and contributed to several books about his experiences, though historians have found that some of his accounts contain inaccuracies. Even so, his later life became a well-known story of change. Fuchida died in 1976. His journey from wartime commander to speaker on peace is often mentioned in discussions of how former enemies came to terms with the past.

arizona-memorial-white-calm-water-mornin.head: The white memorial over the Arizona dips in the middle and rises at both ends, a design chosen deliberately.
arizona-memorial-white-calm-water-mornin.body: The USS Arizona Memorial was designed by the architect Alfred Preis and dedicated in 1962. It spans the sunken hull of the battleship without touching it. The structure is white and about one hundred and eighty-four feet long. Its shape sags in the middle and rises at both ends. Preis explained that the design represented initial defeat and ultimate victory. Inside, a shrine room displays the names of the men who died aboard the Arizona. Visitors reach the memorial by boat from the visitor centre on shore. More than a million people visit each year. Since 1982, some Arizona survivors have chosen to have their ashes placed inside the ship, to rest with their shipmates. Historians and architects consider the memorial one of the most significant in the United States. It is managed by the National Park Service. The ship beneath it is still officially a war grave and remains part of the navy.

oil-drops-rainbow-rings-calm-water.head: Small amounts of oil still rise from the sunken Arizona every day.
oil-drops-rainbow-rings-calm-water.body: The Arizona carried large quantities of fuel oil when it sank in 1941. Small amounts of that oil still escape from the wreck and rise to the surface. Visitors to the memorial can often see drops of oil appearing on the water and spreading into thin, rainbow-coloured films. Some people call them the black tears of the Arizona. The National Park Service and scientists monitor the wreck and the oil leakage. Studies have estimated that a large amount of oil remains inside the hull. Researchers are examining how the steel structure is changing over time, in order to plan for the future. Removing the oil would be extremely difficult without disturbing the ship, which is a war grave. Historians and visitors often describe the rising oil as one of the most moving sights at the memorial. It gives a sense that the ship is still connected to the events of 1941. The drops continue to appear more than eighty years later.

diamond-head-waikiki-evening-surfers.head: Every year on the seventh of December, a moment of silence is observed at Pearl Harbor at five minutes to eight.
diamond-head-waikiki-evening-surfers.body: Each year on the seventh of December, a remembrance ceremony is held at Pearl Harbor. It is organised by the National Park Service and the navy. At five minutes to eight, the time the first bombs fell in 1941, a moment of silence is observed. Ships in the harbour may sound their horns, and military aircraft sometimes fly overhead in a missing-man formation. For many years, survivors of the attack attended and were honoured at the ceremony. As their numbers have declined, their families and younger generations have taken their place. The Pearl Harbor National Memorial includes the Arizona Memorial, the Utah Memorial, the Oklahoma Memorial and other sites. Historians note that the attack is remembered not only in the United States but also in Japan, where it is studied as part of the history of the war. Today, Oahu is once again a place of beaches, surfers and quiet evenings. The ceremony keeps the memory of 1941 alive.
